---
title: "Tutorial"
subtitle: "From nothing to a themed diagram, one step at a time"
---

This page is meant to be followed along with. Every diagram below is rendered
by prism while this page is built — nothing here is a screenshot, and if any
step stopped working the site would fail to build.

## Step 0 — install

```bash
pip install prism-svg
```

The import name is `prism`; the distribution is `prism-svg` because `prism` was
already taken on PyPI. Check it worked:

```bash
prism archetypes
```

You should see ten names. If you have `uv`, `uvx --from prism-svg prism archetypes`
works without installing anything.

## Step 1 — your first diagram

A prism spec is YAML. It needs exactly one thing: a `type`, naming the
archetype. Here is the smallest useful diagram there is.

```{python}
import prism

spec = """
type: flow
steps:
  - label: Draft
  - label: Review
  - label: Ship
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

That is the whole loop: write YAML, get SVG. You never positioned anything —
prism chose the box sizes, the spacing, the arrow geometry and the colours.

Save that YAML to `first.yaml` and you can do the same from a terminal:

```bash
prism render first.yaml -o first.svg
```

## Step 2 — give the nodes some substance

Every archetype in prism consumes the *same* node shape. Learn it once and it
works in all ten. The useful fields are `sublabel`, `icon` and `accent`.

```{python}
spec = """
type: flow
steps:
  - label: Draft
    sublabel: outline + notes
    icon: pencil
    accent: 0
  - label: Review
    sublabel: two readers
    icon: eye
    accent: 1
  - label: Ship
    sublabel: to production
    icon: rocket
    accent: 2
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

`accent` is an index into the theme's colour ramp, **not** a colour. That
indirection is the point: the theme owns the palette, so the same spec restyles
cleanly. There are 1756 icons available (`prism icons`), all from
[Lucide](https://lucide.dev).

## Step 3 — title, subtitle, caption

These live at the top level of the spec, alongside `type`, because they belong
to the diagram rather than to any node.

```{python}
spec = """
type: flow
title: Editorial process
subtitle: for long-form pieces
caption: "Source: the house style guide"
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Ship, icon: rocket, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

That inline `{label: Draft, icon: pencil}` form is ordinary YAML — use whichever
style you find more readable.

## Step 4 — change the direction

Most archetypes take a small number of structural options. `flow` takes
`direction`.

```{python}
spec = """
type: flow
direction: down
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Ship, icon: rocket, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

## Step 5 — pick the archetype by the shape of the meaning

This is the one judgement prism asks of you. Not *what is this about*, but
*what shape is the idea*. The same three-stage editorial process, told as a
loop rather than a line, wants `cycle`:

```{python}
spec = """
type: cycle
title: Editorial loop
center: {label: A piece}
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Revise, icon: wrench, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

And the same content as a judgement about two independent dimensions wants
`quadrant`, where items carry coordinates in `0..1`:

```{python}
spec = """
type: quadrant
title: What to write next
axes:
  x: {label: Effort, low: Low, high: High}
  y: {label: Reach, low: Narrow, high: Wide}
quadrant_labels: [Quick posts, Flagship, Notes, Slog]
items:
  - {label: Weekly note, x: 0.15, y: 0.3}
  - {label: Field guide, x: 0.8, y: 0.85}
  - {label: Talk writeup, x: 0.45, y: 0.6}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

The [catalog](catalog.qmd) shows all ten with the spec that produced each.

## Step 6 — hierarchies, the one recursive case

`hierarchy` is the only archetype whose *data* nests, through `children`. That
is data recursion, not template composition — you still cannot put one
archetype inside another.

```{python}
spec = """
type: hierarchy
title: A book
root:
  label: Manuscript
  icon: book
  children:
    - label: Part I
      children:
        - {label: Chapter 1}
        - {label: Chapter 2}
    - label: Part II
      children:
        - {label: Chapter 3}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

## Step 7 — switch the theme

Add one line. Nothing else about the spec changes.

```{python}
spec = """
type: flow
theme: dark
title: Editorial process
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Ship, icon: rocket, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

Four themes ship: `default`, `dark`, `paper` and `mono`. `paper` is the one to
reach for in print — serif typography, warm surface, hairline strokes:

```{python}
prism.diagram(spec.replace("theme: dark", "theme: paper"))
```

## Step 8 — nudge a single token

You rarely need a whole new theme to change one thing. `tokens:` overrides
individual theme values by dotted path.

```{python}
spec = """
type: flow
theme: paper
tokens:
  geometry.radius: 0
  geometry.gap: 44
title: Wider gaps, square corners
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencil, accent: 0}
  - {label: Review, icon: eye, accent: 1}
  - {label: Ship, icon: rocket, accent: 2}
"""

prism.diagram(spec)
```

A mistyped path fails loudly rather than being ignored — try
`geometry.radiuss` and prism will tell you what it expected.

## Step 9 — your own theme

For a whole document set you want a theme file of your own. Scaffold one:

```bash
prism new-theme house
```

That writes `house.yaml` here, copied from the `default` theme and already
carrying its new name. Start from whichever bundled theme is closest:

```bash
prism new-theme house --from paper      # start from the print theme
prism new-theme house -o themes/house.yaml
```

The file opens with a comment explaining the two rules you have to respect,
so you do not have to remember them. Then point any spec at it:

```yaml
type: flow
theme: ./house.yaml
steps:
  - {label: Draft}
```

Edit the tokens and every diagram that references the file restyles at once.

The two rules, since they surprise people: `typography.family` must be
`grotesque`, `serif` or `mono`, and `typography.weight` values must be `400`
or `700`. Those are exactly the fonts and weights whose metrics prism has
vendored. Anything else would mean measuring text against a font your reader
does not have, and labels would overflow their boxes. `prism new-theme`
validates the file it writes, so a bad edit fails when you next render rather
than producing a quietly broken picture.

## Step 10 — when something is wrong

prism's errors are written to be acted on. Each names the bad value and points
at the valid neighbours.

```{python}
#| error: true
prism.render_str("""
type: flow
steps:
  - {label: Draft, icon: pencl}
""")
```

The same holds for unknown archetypes, unknown theme tokens, and dangling
references such as a `matrix` cell naming a row that does not exist.

## Step 11 — put it in your own Quarto document

Everything above is a real Quarto page. The pattern is:

````markdown
```{{python}}
#| label: fig-process
#| fig-cap: "The editorial process"
#| echo: false
import prism
prism.diagram("figures/process.yaml")
```
````

`prism.diagram()` accepts a path or a spec string and returns an object that
knows how to display itself, so Quarto embeds the SVG directly — no
intermediate file and no rasterisation. See [In Quarto](quarto.qmd) for PDF
output and batch rendering.
